opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The starting point is noticing that a lot of the strategic structure we had during the nuclear era carries over, even though AI is a very different technology. With nuclear weapons, the key insight wasn't "let's build the biggest arsenal and win." It was that once both sides had a destabilizing capability, the stable outcome was deterrence. Neither side could make a bid for dominance without the other responding in a way that made the whole thing catastrophic.

So in the framework I've worked on with colleagues, we organize things around three pillars that loosely mirror nuclear strategy: deterrence, nonproliferation, and competitiveness.

On deterrence, the analogue to mutual assured destruction is what we've called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction, or MAIM. The idea is that if any state makes an aggressive bid for unilateral dominance, say racing toward a superintelligence that would give it a decisive strategic advantage, its rivals have strong incentives to sabotage that project. That could mean cyberattacks on training runs, degrading datacenters, or more overt measures. Because AI projects are fairly fragile and depend on big, visible infrastructure, that sabotage is quite feasible. So you get a deterrence regime that already exists implicitly, whether or not anyone declares it. The strategic goal is to make it stable: clear escalation ladders, transparency so states don't misread each other, maybe even placing datacenters away from population centers, the way we thought about counterforce versus countervalue targeting.

Nonproliferation is the second piece. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviets were rivals, but they agreed it was bad for fissile material to end up with rogue actors. With AI, the analogues are compute, model weights, and certain hazardous capabilities like bioweapons expertise. So you want export controls on advanced chips, good tracking of where chips end up, strong information security around weights, and technical safeguards so models don't hand out expert-level virology help to anyone who asks. Great powers can cooperate on that even while competing elsewhere.

Competitiveness is the third pillar. Deterrence doesn't mean disarmament. States will still want economic and military strength from AI, so it's about domestic chip manufacturing, integrating AI into the military responsibly, and legal frameworks for AI agents, so you're not falling behind.

Where the analogy breaks down matters a lot. Nuclear weapons don't make decisions, and they don't recursively improve themselves. AI has a loss-of-control risk with no clean nuclear counterpart. That's partly why I think a bid for superintelligence is destabilizing even for the state attempting it: you might win the race and lose control. And AI capabilities are much more diffuse and dual-use than enriched uranium, so nonproliferation is harder in some ways.

But the core lesson holds: in a world of destabilizing technologies, safety comes less from one actor winning and more from a stable equilibrium where nobody has the incentive to make a reckless bid for dominance. That's what I'm trying to translate into the AI context.

r001.rationale: It identifies advanced-chip export controls as part of AI nonproliferation and compares AI controls to Cold War controls on fissile material.

r002.rationale: It mentions US-Soviet rivalry and AI competition among states, but does not present competition with China as the counterpart to containing the Soviet Union.

r003.rationale: It discusses domestic chip manufacturing and avoiding falling behind, but does not define competitive success as global market share rather than building superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the nuclear analogy is useful but you have to be careful with it, because the structures aren't identical and people tend to either over-apply it or dismiss it entirely. What I take from the nuclear era is mostly a way of thinking about strategic stability rather than any specific policy copied over wholesale.

So in the paper with Eric Schmidt and Alex Wang, the central concept we introduced was Mutual Assured AI Malfunction, or MAIM, which is deliberately an echo of mutual assured destruction. The core observation is this: if one state makes a bid for a decisive strategic advantage through AI, something like a recursive self-improvement loop or an intelligence explosion that would let it dominate everyone else, its rivals are not going to sit there and accept that. They have the capability to sabotage it. Data centers are not hardened. You can do cyberattacks on training runs, you can interfere with the chip supply, you can go after the physical infrastructure, and in the extreme case there's kinetic action. The point is that destabilizing AI projects are deterrable by default, in the same way that a first strike was deterrable because of second-strike capability. And once you recognize that, you realize there's already a kind of deterrence regime in place whether anyone has articulated it or not. The question is whether we make it stable or leave it to accident.

The nuclear era teaches you that stability doesn't come from good intentions, it comes from structure. You want transparency measures, you want clear red lines, you want communication channels so that misperception doesn't lead to escalation. In the Cold War you had hotlines, you had arms control verification, you had a mutual understanding of what counted as a provocation. We're going to need analogues for that. For example, states should be able to distinguish between a lab doing ordinary commercial development and a lab that's attempting a superweapon-scale project. Datacenter locations, compute concentrations, those become the strategically relevant facts, the way missile silos were.

The second piece I borrow is nonproliferation. With fissile material, the whole regime rested on the fact that enrichment is a bottleneck you can monitor. With AI, the analogue is compute. Advanced chips are the uranium of this era. So export controls and chip tracking, knowing where the high-end hardware is and who's using it, that's the nonproliferation layer. It's about keeping catastrophic capabilities, bioweapons assistance, large-scale cyberattacks, out of the hands of rogue actors and terrorists, which is a separate problem from great-power competition.

And the third piece is competitiveness, which is where the analogy actually breaks down somewhat. Nuclear weapons didn't make your economy grow. AI does. So you can't just freeze everything the way some people want. States are going to pursue it for economic and military reasons, and pretending otherwise is not a strategy. The realistic goal is to channel that competition so it doesn't tip into a destabilizing race for a monopoly on power.

Where I'd push back on the lazy version of the analogy is the idea that there's a single Manhattan Project moment and whoever gets there first wins. That framing is actively dangerous, because it's exactly the kind of bid that invites preemption. The nuclear lesson, properly understood, isn't "build the bomb first." It's that once multiple actors have the capability to hurt each other badly, the rational move is to establish a regime of mutual restraint rather than gamble everything on a sprint that your adversary will try to sabotage halfway through.

r001.rationale: It describes export controls and tracking advanced chips as the AI nonproliferation layer, analogous to monitoring fissile material.

r002.rationale: It does not identify competition with China as a counterpart to containing the Soviet Union.

r003.rationale: It rejects a race to build superintelligence first and discusses economic competition, but does not define success as global market share for a country's AI systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that deterrence is still relevant, but we shouldn’t assume AI competition will look exactly like nuclear competition. With nuclear weapons, you have relatively identifiable assets and a fairly clear threshold for their use. AI is much more diffuse. It’s integrated into the economy, it can proliferate through software, and its capabilities can change quite quickly.

So one idea to adapt is mutual assured destruction into mutual assured malfunction: creating a situation where no actor can confidently use an advanced AI system to achieve decisive dominance, because other actors have credible ways to disrupt that attempt. The purpose would be to discourage a reckless bid for power, rather than simply to win a race to build the most capable system.

But deterrence alone isn’t sufficient. You also want agreements around shared risks, ways to verify compliance, and communication that prevents an accident from becoming an escalation. The lesson from the nuclear era is that competitors can have very serious conflicts of interest and still cooperate to avoid outcomes that are disastrous for everyone.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deterrence, disruption, agreements, and verification, but does not identify AI chip export controls or compare them with fissile-material controls.

r002.rationale: It refers generally to competing actors and conflicts of interest, without naming China or presenting competition with China as analogous to containment of the Soviet Union.

r003.rationale: It does not define success as global market share for a country's AI systems or contrast that goal with being first to build superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate the logic of deterrence from the particular features of nuclear weapons. The useful lesson is that pursuing an advantage can make everyone less secure if it creates pressure to race, conceal capabilities, or strike first.

For AI, one possibility is what we call mutual assured AI malfunction. The idea is that states could deter rivals from pursuing a destabilizing AI project if they could credibly threaten to disrupt it, potentially through cyber operations. That could make a unilateral bid for overwhelming power less attractive.

But that’s a proposal with serious risks, not a guarantee of stability. AI systems are much harder to monitor than missile silos, and interference can be misinterpreted or cause escalation. So you also need diplomacy, verification where it’s feasible, and agreements around dangerous capabilities. The objective is to change the incentives so that restraint is compatible with national security, rather than asking countries simply to trust one another.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI deterrence and cyber disruption but does not identify chip export controls as an analogue to fissile-material nonproliferation controls.

r002.rationale: It does not mention China or present competition with China as analogous to nuclear-era containment of the Soviet Union.

r003.rationale: It discusses incentives and restraint but does not frame success as global market share rather than being first to build superintelligence.
